title: National Assembly Sends Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill to State Legislatures to Enable State Police
text:
The National Assembly has forwarded the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill, which seeks to authorize the creation of state police forces, to all 36 State Houses of Assembly. The bill now awaits approval by at least two‑thirds of the state legislatures as required by the Constitution before it can be enacted.
The decision to move the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill to the state houses marks a pivotal step in Nigeria's ongoing debate over the establishment of state police forces.
The bill, which has already been endorsed by both the Senate and the House of Representatives, is now in the hands of the 36 state legislatures for their consideration and final approval. According to Article 9 of the Constitution, a federal constitutional amendment requires the approval of at least two‑thirds of the state Houses of Assembly before it can be introduced to the National Assembly for final passage.
Chief Clerk Kamoru Ogunlana announced that the National Assembly has complied with its constitutional duty by transmitting the bill to each state legislature as of 16 September 2026. While the Constitution does not dictate a specific deadline for the state assemblies to complete their review, the Assembly leadership has requested that the review be finished within 30 days to keep the process on schedule.
The clerk's statement emphasized that the 30‑day period is an administrative guideline rather than a legal mandate, and that the state legislatures retain full discretion in setting their own timetable. The clerk further urged each state to adopt its standard legislative procedures and to submit resolutions to Parliament in a timely fashion.
The bill proposes to amply draft the provisions that would allow state governments to form and deploy police forces under their own jurisdiction, thereby decentralising a significant component of law enforcement from the Federal Police. If ratified, the amendment would lead to a re‑organisation of policing responsibilities at both the federal and state levels. State police could be tasked with maintaining order in local communities, providing first‑response services and cooperating with federal agencies for national security concerns.
The bill also outlines guidelines for funding, training, equipment and operational oversight to ensure that state police units meet national standards. The National Assembly's transmission of the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill reflects the Assembly's recognition of the constitutional principle that amendments involving the structure of the union must be discussed at all levels of government.
The six‑year cycle for constitutional amendments gives states the opportunity to deliberate on the implications of structural changes as well as to align state policies with federal objectives. The Congress has stated that it will continue to urge the state legislatures to convey their resolutions as soon as possible, and that it will prepare for the subsequent legislative steps upon receipt.
In addition to the state police provision, the Constitution (Sixth Alteration) Bill also addresses other significant subjects, such as electoral reforms and the status of oil‑rich zones. Some of those provisions remain under deliberation and will be presented to the state assemblies in separate packages. The National Assembly's primary concern remains ensuring that any amendments comply with established constitutional protocols and that political actors on all levels demonstrate a shared commitment to strengthening governance.
The move has sparked spirited discussions within political circles. Supporters argue that localised security forces would bring police closer to the communities they serve, potentially improving responsiveness and trust. Critics caution that additional layers of policing may lead to duplication of authority and confusion over jurisdiction. Nonetheless, there is a broad consensus that any change to the national security structure must undergo rigorous democratic scrutiny.
The National Assembly's communication plan ensures transparency during the transition. A dedicated portal will be established where the public can track the status of each state legislature's vote and review the official resolutions submitted.
Moreover, a committee of constitutional experts will audit the procedural aspects of the amendment's passage to guard against procedural irregularities. This structure underscores the Assembly's confidence in the capacity of Nigeria's legislative system to evolve while preserving democratic integrity
